headline.headline: GUARDIANS STORM BACK WITH FIVE-RUN EIGHTH TO STUN MARINERS
headline.deck: Cleveland rallies from four-run deficit to edge Seattle 6-5 at Progressive Field
headline.body:
CLEVELAND — The Seattle Mariners held a 4-1 lead walking into the bottom of the eighth inning at Progressive Field on Sunday and appeared to be moments away from a series win. The Cleveland Guardians had other ideas. Cleveland erupted for five runs in the eighth to turn a three-run deficit into a 6-5 victory before 27,934 fans, delivering one of the most stunning reversals of the baseball weekend.

Seattle had built its cushion methodically, scoring once in the second, twice in the third and once more in the sixth while holding Cleveland to a single run through seven innings. The Guardians' offense had been largely dormant, but the eighth inning became a full collapse for the Mariners bullpen. Cleveland sent enough batters to the plate to push across five runs and seize a lead it would not relinquish. Josh Naylor, who had been hit by a pitch from Herrin earlier in the contest, was at the center of the Cleveland lineup's late charge.

Seattle managed one final run in the ninth inning, cutting the deficit back to one, but Cleveland closer held firm to preserve the 6-5 final. The Guardians improved their standing in the AL Central with the comeback victory, while the Mariners left Ohio having squandered what seemed an eminently winnable afternoon. It was the kind of eighth inning that will haunt a pitching staff for days.

secondary.headline: NATIONALS RALLY PAST ORIOLES IN BATTLE OF BELTWAY
secondary.deck: Washington scores six after falling behind 2-0, hands Baltimore a costly home loss
secondary.body:
BALTIMORE — The Washington Nationals trailed by two runs after the first inning at Oriole Park at Camden Yards and then proceeded to outscore Baltimore 6-2 over the final eight innings, walking away with a 6-4 victory before 27,626 fans on Sunday afternoon. The Nationals put up three runs in the third inning to seize the lead and added two more in the fifth and one in the seventh to build enough cushion to survive a late Baltimore push in the seventh.

The Orioles, who drew first blood with a two-run first, could not recover from the third-inning implosion that flipped the game's momentum entirely. Baltimore managed two runs in the seventh but got nothing in the eighth or ninth. The loss stings for a Baltimore club trying to climb the AL East standings, while Washington heads to Boston to open a three-game set against the Red Sox carrying genuine confidence after a complete-game team performance in 2 hours and 55 minutes of play.

secondary.headline: ASTROS OUTLAST TIGERS IN TEN AS DE LOS SANTOS DELIVERS
secondary.deck: Houston scores four in the tenth inning to beat Detroit 7-5 and avoid overtime collapse
secondary.body:
DETROIT — Houston entered the tenth inning tied 3-3 with the Detroit Tigers at Comerica Park and left with a 7-5 victory, scoring four runs in the extra frame to put away a Tigers club that had led for much of the afternoon. Detroit had taken a 2-0 lead in the second inning and added a run in the fifth before Houston's offense finally awoke with two runs in the seventh and one in the eighth to force extra innings. The game consumed 3 hours and 32 minutes, with Enmanuel De Los Santos earning the win in relief.

Jack Flaherty was also credited in the winning decision as the Astros navigated a bullpen effort through the final innings. Detroit pushed two runs across in the tenth to briefly make it a game before Houston's four-run outburst ended the drama. The Tigers fell to 35-49 on the season and now open a three-game road series at Yankee Stadium beginning Monday, where the 48-35 Yankees await.

secondary.headline: BILLS DRAW LINE ON O.J. SIMPSON AT NEW STADIUM
secondary.deck: Buffalo will not honor former running back among franchise legends when new venue opens
secondary.body:
BUFFALO — The Buffalo Bills announced Sunday that O.J. Simpson will not be recognized among the franchise's legends when the team's new stadium opens its doors. The decision closes a long and uncomfortable chapter for a franchise that once celebrated Simpson as one of its greatest players but has grown increasingly reluctant to attach his name to its identity in any official capacity.

The announcement drew immediate reaction across the league. Simpson, who rushed for 10,183 yards during his time in Buffalo and was a five-time Pro Bowl selection with the Bills, remains one of the most statistically significant players in franchise history. The team offered no detailed public statement beyond confirming the exclusion. The new stadium represents a fresh start for the organization, and the Bills clearly intend that fresh start to carry a firm boundary.

column.headline: CLEVELAND'S FIFTH-RUN EIGHTH SHOULD REMIND EVERY TEAM: NEVER HAND THE GAME AWAY
column.body:
Five runs in one inning when your bullpen has a three-run lead in the eighth. That is not a statistical anomaly. That is a managerial and personnel failure of the first order. The Seattle Mariners walked into Progressive Field on Sunday, held the Guardians to one run through seven innings, and then watched their relievers turn a winning afternoon into a 6-5 loss. There is no charitable interpretation of what happened in that eighth inning, and the Mariners' front office should be asking hard questions about the depth of arms available in the late innings.

The Cleveland comeback deserves full credit, but it takes two teams to produce a collapse of that magnitude. The Guardians did not steal the game so much as the Mariners handed it over and asked them to please sign for the package. With the AL playoff picture tightening and Seattle needing every win it can find, surrendering a five-run lead over a single inning is the kind of gut punch that echoes into September standings. The baseball weekend produced no shortage of drama, but nothing cut quite as deep as what happened in Cleveland's eighth.

story.headline: PHILLIES HOLD OFF METS AS SCHWARBER SLUGS NO. 30
story.deck: Philadelphia survives late New York rally to take cross-division road win
story.body:
NEW YORK — Kyle Schwarber crushed his 30th home run of the season and the Philadelphia Phillies survived a three-run Mets rally in the sixth inning to escape Citi Field with a 5-4 victory Sunday, as Philadelphia's bullpen slammed the door over the final three frames before 38,770 fans.

The Phillies staked themselves to a 3-0 lead with a three-run third inning, and Schwarber's milestone blast gave Philadelphia breathing room heading into the middle innings. The Mets clawed back in the sixth on a pinch-hit home run by Taylor, T, who connected after Vientos struck out, cutting the deficit to 3-4 before the Phillies answered with two runs in the seventh on a home run by Ewing, his fourth of the year, to push the lead to 5-4. New York managed nothing against the Philadelphia relief corps in the eighth or ninth, stranding a staggering 31 runners on base across the full game.

The loss left New York searching for answers after squandering numerous opportunities all evening. Trea Turner and Schwarber each swiped a base for Philadelphia, and Alec Bohm, Brandon Marsh, and Francisco Alvarez contributed doubles in a game that featured heavy traffic on the bases from both sides. The Phillies improve their position in the NL East race while the Mets, loaded with baserunners but short on clutch hitting, absorbed a defeat that will sting deep into the week.

story.headline: HORNETS SHIP MILES BRIDGES TO PHOENIX IN BLOCKBUSTER DEAL AS NBA OFFSEASON RESHAPES THE WEST
story.deck: Charlotte sends Bridges and draft capital to Suns in a move signaling a full rebuild.
story.body:
The Charlotte Hornets have agreed to trade forward Miles Bridges to the Phoenix Suns, according to league sources, a deal that strips one of the franchise's most recognizable faces and signals an unmistakable pivot toward a full-scale rebuild around LaMelo Ball. In return, Charlotte receives Grayson Allen and additional compensation, a haul that gives head coach and front office architects fresh roster flexibility heading into one of the most turbulent free agency periods the league has seen in years.

Bridges, 28, averaged a career-high 23.1 points per game last season while shooting 47 percent from the field, numbers that made him one of the more attractive trade chips available on the market. Phoenix, searching for reliable wing scoring and physicality after a disappointing 2025-26 campaign, lands a proven scorer who can play alongside Devin Booker in a retooled Western Conference rotation. The Suns also absorb a 2029 first-round pick and a second-round selection as part of the package, suggesting Charlotte drove a hard negotiation despite the franchise moving on.

The broader offseason picture around the league remains volatile. NBA trade tracker updates show multiple front offices maneuvering below the second apron, with cap analyst Bobby Marks noting that fewer than a handful of teams carry genuine max-contract spending power this summer. For the Hornets, the Bridges deal clears the decks and places the organizational vision squarely on Ball's shoulders, a franchise-altering bet that Charlotte is wagering will pay dividends well before that 2029 pick ever changes hands.

story.headline: SHARKS MAKE HISTORY WITH 7-FOOT-1 KARMANOV, PREDATORS LOCK UP DRURY AS WILD 2026 DRAFT WEEKEND WRAPS
story.deck: San Jose selects tallest player ever drafted; Nashville wastes no time securing faceoff specialist.
story.body:
SAN JOSE — The 2026 NHL Draft produced a moment for the record books Sunday when the San Jose Sharks selected Russian defenseman Alexander Karmanov with a pick that instantly rewrote history. The 18-year-old Karmanov, standing an extraordinary 7 feet 1 inch tall, became the tallest player ever chosen in the 109-year history of the league, a distinction that drew gasps from the draft floor and set social media ablaze within minutes of the announcement. General manager Mike Grier called Karmanov a generational defensive presence whose sheer reach and skating development could redefine the Sharks blue line for years to come.

Meanwhile, in Nashville, the Predators moved swiftly to capitalize on the weekend's momentum by signing forward Jack Drury to a five-year contract worth $22.5 million, just four days after claiming him in the draft. Drury, widely regarded as one of the premier faceoff specialists in his draft class, gives Nashville a reliable center-ice presence as the franchise pushes to rebuild around a harder, more competitive identity. The deal signals that Predators management is not content to let top prospects linger in prolonged negotiations.

Across the league, draft grades were already flowing in fast and furious, with the New York Rangers, Toronto Maple Leafs and Chicago Blackhawks drawing the most attention from analysts dissecting the weekend's winners and losers. The Rangers earned particular praise for a draft haul built on depth and positional need, while certain franchises faced sharp criticism for reaching on prospects with significant developmental question marks. Fantasy hockey managers, meanwhile, scrambled to identify which top picks deserved roster spots heading into next season, with Karmanov and Drury both generating immediate buzz.

story.headline: QUARTERBACK CAROUSEL SPINS WILDLY AS TEAMS RETOOL FOR 2026 CAMPAIGN
story.deck: Several franchises are reshaping their rosters this spring with bold moves at the position.
story.body:
The NFL offseason has shifted into high gear this May, with multiple franchises making aggressive moves to secure their franchise quarterbacks before training camps open in late July. The Cleveland Browns made the most dramatic splash, acquiring veteran signal-caller Sam Darnold from the Minnesota Vikings in exchange for a package that included two second-round picks, giving Cleveland its most experienced starter in years after another disappointing finish to the 2025 season.

The Las Vegas Raiders continued their rebuild under second-year head coach Mike Vrabel by signing former Pittsburgh Steelers backup Kyle Allen to a two-year bridge deal, buying time while the organization evaluates its options ahead of what scouts project will be a quarterback-rich 2027 draft class. Meanwhile, the Carolina Panthers have generated significant buzz after agreeing to terms with free agent wide receiver Stefon Diggs, pairing the veteran pass-catcher with young quarterback Bryce Young in what the organization hopes will be a rejuvenating connection for both players.

Draft analysts continue to dissect the results of last month's NFL Draft, where the Tennessee Titans used the fourth overall pick on Colorado wide receiver Travis Hunter Jr., a versatile playmaker who drew comparisons to Deion Sanders for his ability to contribute on both sides of the ball at the collegiate level. NFL Network draft guru Daniel Jeremiah called the selection the boldest pick of the entire first round, noting that no team had asked a player to play meaningful offensive and defensive snaps simultaneously at the professional level in more than two decades.
